It's been almost a decade since I've heard of lojban. That's pretty cool. Does it ever evolve or fork. I have a criticism of it. Hopefully more interesting than critical.

So about the punctuation being at the front of the sentence. Reminds me of a topic in programming. So the new line character. Some inexperienced programmers think that the way it works is you write a line and if you want a new line that's what the new line character is for. When you read the posix spec you get a different story. Something is not considered a line unless it is terminated with a new line, or rather an EOL, end of line character. So why did they do that when they had their choice. Because it removes any ambiguity of considering if their might be more. I know lojban tries to reduce ambiguity and be more like a language a computer would use. The EOL character reduces the amount of code we have to right because it is straight forward (particularly for tcp streams), and lojban considers that having less interperative complexity makes language easier to read so what is good for one would be good for the other.

So it's not the most intense of situations for a human language. Humans can handle a period at the beginning. But it brings us to a more meta-discussion. If the most logical way to do something takes time to discover how does lojban repent from a mistake? In the python world a dogma of "we do things better, we code things right. There is only one right way to code and it's our semantics" has been considered a language feature. The problem is when anti-patterns end up in the semantics early on like print something vs print(something). One is more forwards compatible and objectively better, when the intention of preaching the former as the preferred semantic was only meant to produce consistence for an issue that didn't really matter, where consistency itself offered more value.

How does lojban correct it's own anti-patterns? Surely they have to exist?
